cards.front: What is a port, and why do networked systems use port numbers?
cards.back:
A port is a number (0–65,535) embedded in a network packet header that tells the operating system which application should receive the packet.

An IP address identifies the machine. The port number identifies the application on that machine.

A server running a web application, an SSH daemon, and a database simultaneously needs a way to route incoming traffic to the right program. When a packet arrives, the OS reads the port number and delivers it to the registered application.

Analogy: IP address = the building. Port number = the department number inside the building.
cards.hint: IP = building address. Port = department number. Without port numbers, all traffic would pile up at the front door.

cards.front: What are the three port states in a TCP SYN scan — and what does each mean at the packet level?
cards.back:
OPEN: Your SYN reached a listening service. SYN/ACK came back — the port is open and active. Something is home.

CLOSED: Your SYN reached the host, but no service is on this port. RST came back from the host itself — a definitive 'nothing here.' The host is alive; this door is empty.

FILTERED: Your SYN was blocked before it reached the host. No response arrived. The port state — open or closed — cannot be determined.

Professional response:
Open → fingerprint and test
Closed → document, move on
Filtered → document carefully, investigate further, never mark as safe
cards.hint: SYN/ACK = open. RST from host = closed. Silence = filtered (unknown, not safe).

cards.front: How does the TCP SYN scan work, and why is it the professional default?
cards.back:
The SYN scan sends a SYN packet to each port and analyses the response:
• SYN/ACK → port open (service listening)
• RST → port closed (host alive, nothing here)
• No response → port filtered (probe blocked)

After receiving SYN/ACK, Nmap immediately sends RST to tear down the half-open connection — never completing the three-way handshake.

Why it is the professional default:
1. Fast — no session maintenance, no full connections
2. Reduced footprint — many application logs record only completed connections
3. Reliable — all three states are clearly distinguishable
4. Standard — universally understood by security professionals

Requires root or administrator privileges.
cards.hint: SYN sent → response analysed → RST sent immediately. Handshake never completes.

cards.front: What does 'filtered' mean, and why is it not the same as 'nothing there'?
cards.back:
Filtered means the SYN probe was intercepted by a firewall before reaching the host. No response was received within the timeout window.

Filtered contains two possible realities:
1. A service IS running behind the filter — reachable from trusted networks but not from your scanning position
2. The port is empty — but the firewall happens to be blocking it anyway

From outside the firewall, these look identical. You cannot distinguish them with a SYN scan.

Why it matters: management interfaces, databases, and administrative panels frequently live on filtered ports. A firewall rule was specifically written for this port — which means someone decided it needed protection.

Professional response: document precisely, investigate alternative probes, report as unknown — never as cleared.
cards.hint: Filtered = probe blocked = state unknown. A guard in front of a door does not prove the room is empty.

cards.front: The service column in Nmap output shows 'http' on port 80 and 'mysql' on port 3306. What do these labels actually tell you?
cards.back:
They tell you: Nmap looked up those port numbers in the IANA port number registry and found the conventional service assignment.

Port 80 → conventionally HTTP
Port 3306 → conventionally MySQL

They do NOT tell you:
• What software is actually running on these ports
• What version of the software is installed
• How the service is configured
• Whether the service matches the label at all

A web application running on port 3000 would show as 'ppp' (a dial-up protocol — the IANA assignment). A database on a non-standard port would show an unrelated label.

Service labels are starting hypotheses. Confirmed service identity requires fingerprinting (Mission 3).
cards.hint: Label = IANA convention for the port number. Identity = what fingerprinting confirms is actually running.

cards.front: Why run a full-range scan (-p-) in addition to the default scan? When should you do it?
cards.back:
The default Nmap scan covers roughly 1,000 ports based on historical frequency data — not ports 1 through 1,000. Approximately 64,535 ports are not checked.

Services on non-standard ports — management interfaces, legacy applications, forgotten administrative tools — are precisely what lives outside the default range. The case study showed: port 8443, outside the default range, hosting a management panel with default credentials.

When to run the full-range scan:
• On every confirmed high-priority target
• After the default scan shows interesting services worth investigating thoroughly
• Whenever you need to state with confidence that the full port space was assessed

Command: nmap -sS -p- -T4 -oA fullscan-[ip] [ip]

Document what you scanned in every report.
cards.hint: Default = fast + high-yield. Not complete. Full range = -p-. Always run on high-priority targets.

cards.front: What is the professional port scanning workflow on a real engagement?
cards.back:
1. Confirm targets — only hosts verified alive from host discovery
2. Default scan — nmap -sS -T4 -oA port-scan-[ip] [ip]: quick initial picture
3. Full-range scan — nmap -sS -p- on every high-priority target
4. Document all three states separately — open, closed, filtered (never grouped)
5. Flag filtered for follow-up — investigate with alternative probes, never mark as safe
6. Note service labels — preliminary hypotheses for fingerprinting next
7. Build the port map — the input for Mission 3 service fingerprinting

Save every output file. Name files with target IP and scan type.
cards.hint: Confirm → Default → Full-range → Document all three states → Flag filtered → Fingerprint next.
